question: On the last day of school, Mrs. Wonderful gave jelly beans to her class. She gave each boy as many jelly beans as there were boys in the class. She gave each girl as many jelly beans as there were girls in the class. She brought \(400\) jelly beans, and when she finished, she had six jelly beans left. There were two more boys than girls in her class. How many students were in her class?
solution:
Mrs. Wonderful gave away \(400-6=394\) jelly beans. Each group's bean total is its number of students multiplied by itself, because every student receives that same number of beans.

Half of \(394\) is \(197\), close to \(14\cdot14=196\), so look for group sizes near \(14\). With two more boys than girls, try \(13\) girls and \(15\) boys. Their bean totals are
\[
13\cdot13+15\cdot15=169+225=394.
\]
This is the only possible pair. Fewer than \(13\) girls would also mean fewer than \(15\) boys, making both bean totals smaller. More than \(13\) girls would make both totals larger. Thus the class had \(13+15=28\) students, choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

reference.question: On the last day of school, Mrs. Wonderful gave jelly beans to her class. She gave each boy as many jelly beans as there were boys in the class. She gave each girl as many jelly beans as there were girls in the class. She brought \(400\) jelly beans, and when she finished, she had six jelly beans left. There were two more boys than girls in her class. How many students were in her class?
reference.solution:
Method 1: Compare nearby group sizes

Mrs. Wonderful gave away \(400-6=394\) jelly beans. Each group's bean total is its number of students multiplied by itself, because every student receives that same number of beans.

Half of \(394\) is \(197\), close to \(14\cdot14=196\), so look for group sizes near \(14\). With two more boys than girls, try \(13\) girls and \(15\) boys. Their bean totals are
\[
13\cdot13+15\cdot15=169+225=394.
\]
This is the only possible pair. Fewer than \(13\) girls would also mean fewer than \(15\) boys, making both bean totals smaller. More than \(13\) girls would make both totals larger. Thus the class had \(13+15=28\) students, choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
